hints: Focus on what actually has to be broken when a simple molecular solid like chlorine or iodine melts.
Remember both $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$ are non-polar, so think about what only type of intermolecular force holds them together.
Consider how more electrons and a larger electron cloud in iodine affects how easily temporary dipoles can form and attract.
walkthrough:
**Separate what is broken from what is kept**

Think of melting as pulling molecules apart from each other, not breaking molecules apart inside. The strong covalent $\text{Cl-Cl}$ and $\text{I-I}$ bonds stay intact, only the weak forces between molecules are overcome.

**Identify the force between halogen molecules**

Both $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$ are non-polar diatomic molecules, so they have no permanent dipoles. The only attraction between them is instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces, also called London dispersion forces.

**Compare chlorine and iodine**

Iodine atoms are much larger with many more electrons than chlorine, so the electron cloud is more easily distorted. This gives stronger temporary dipoles and stronger attractions, so more energy is needed to separate $\text{I}_2$ molecules, giving a higher melting point.

options.A: Incorrect. Melting does not break covalent bonds, it only overcomes intermolecular forces. In fact the $\text{I-I}$ covalent bond is longer and weaker than the $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond, so this cannot explain the higher melting point.
options.B: Incorrect. Both $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$ are symmetrical non-polar molecules with zero permanent dipole moment. There are no permanent dipole-dipole forces to compare here.
options.C: Incorrect. Volatility is the ease of evaporating, which is the opposite trend. Because iodine has a higher melting and boiling point, it is less volatile than chlorine, not more.
options.D: Correct. Iodine has many more electrons and a larger, more polarisable electron cloud than chlorine. This creates stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London dispersion) forces between $\text{I}_2$ molecules, requiring more energy to separate them, hence the higher melting point.
